analysis.one_liner: Tightens the rules on how long insurers can deny or delay coverage for pre-existing conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate health committee in October 2007, never received a vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the rules then in effect, health plans could look back six months into a person's medical history and refuse to cover a pre-existing condition for up to a year. This bill would have cut that look-back to 30 days, capped any exclusion period at three months, extended the same limits to individual-market insurance policies, and dropped a requirement that people first use up their old employer coverage before getting new protections. It was never taken up by the committee it was sent to.
analysis.who_benefits: People with health problems who change jobs or buy their own insurance. Under the rules of the time, a six-month look-back and up to a year of exclusions could leave someone's cancer, diabetes, or pregnancy treatment unpaid for a year after switching plans. Shortening the look-back to 30 days and the exclusion to three months, and applying those limits to individual policies, would have sharply reduced how long a gap in coverage could cost them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with pre-existing conditions between jobs

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the window insurers can use to search a new enrollee's medical history from six months to 30 days, in group plans, individual policies, and the tax code provisions that mirror them.
Caps any pre-existing condition exclusion at three months (nine months for someone who signs up late), down from 12 and 18 months.
Extends the group-plan limits to health insurance sold in the individual market, where exclusions had previously been governed by separate, weaker rules.
Removes the requirement that a person must have elected and exhausted COBRA continuation coverage before qualifying for protections when buying individual coverage.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, who would lose part of their ability to price or restrict coverage based on a customer's medical history, and to the extent costs shift, enrollees in group and individual plans through premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and, partly, plan enrollees

drawbacks.text: The bill narrows but does not eliminate pre-existing condition exclusions, and it does not require insurers to sell a policy to someone with a serious condition in the first place, so a person could still be turned down entirely in the individual market.

Restricting how insurers can use medical history without also mandating that everyone carry coverage can push healthier people to wait until they are sick to buy insurance, which insurers argued would raise premiums for everyone — a cost that would fall partly on ordinary enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with chronic or costly conditions, the benefit is concrete and immediate: months or years of uncovered treatment become covered. The main cost is higher premiums spread across everyone in a plan, and the main weakness is that the bill leaves the underlying practice of excluding pre-existing conditions in place rather than ending it — a half-measure that fell well short of what Congress ultimately enacted in 2010.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Rockefeller IV introduced the bill on October 25, 2007, with no cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; no further action appears in the record.
No markup, committee vote, floor debate, or roll call ever occurred, and the bill expired with the end of the 110th Congress in January 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, who kept the full six-month look-back and up-to-a-year exclusion periods that the bill would have shortened.

for.name: Sen. John Rockefeller IV
for.role: Sponsor, U.S. Senator from West Virginia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would cut insurers' ability to use a customer's medical history to deny or delay paying for care — shrinking a six-month look-back to 30 days and exclusion periods from a year to three months. That profit channel came directly at sick patients' expense, so insurers' interest ran against the people the bill was written for.

industries.industry: Employers and group health plan sponsors
industries.note: Employers sponsoring group plans would have had to comply with the shorter look-back and exclusion caps, a compliance change phased in over roughly a year, but their enrollees — the same workers they cover — were the bill's beneficiaries.
